newsitem.title: USA: Fran a formidable foe for N.Carolina election race.
newsitem.headline: Fran a formidable foe for N.Carolina election race.

text.p: Candidates have fought hard this election season to succeed retiring 24-year Representative Charlie Rose, even having to overcome two hurricanes that distracted already apathetic voters.

For all his problems -- scandal, divorce and accusations of campaign finance impropriety and voter fraud -- Democrat Rose's seniority will be a tough act for any successor to follow. Since taking office in 1972 he steadily amassed power and influence on Capitol Hill.

Rose was chairman of the Tobacco and Peanuts Subcommittee, where he successfully fought for tobacco farm interests and fought off a cigarette tax plan to finance President Bill Clinton's doomed 1992 healthcare reform package.

But since Rose announced he would not seek reelection, voters have demonstrated little interest in who takes his place, even though political observers have called the election an important battle in Democrats' bid to regain control of the House and Republicans' fight to keep it.
"I don't think anybody is interested in who gets elected," said Lee Johnston, a political scientist at the University of North Carolina at Wilmington.

The May 7 primary generated an anaemic 25 percent voter turnout and Democrats Mike McIntyre and Rose Marie Lowry-Townsend and Republicans Robert Anderson and Bill Caster drew only a 10 percent turnout for the June 4 runoff.

Two remarkably similar candidates emerged as winners, as conservative Democrat McIntyre defeated liberal Lowry-Townsend, and moderate Republican Caster beat conservative Anderson by identical 54 to 46 percent margins.

McIntyre, 40, a Lumberton attorney, said the choice came down to which candidate was most accessible and accountable. Caster, 56, a Wilmington businessman and retired Coast Guard captain, said his education and experience as a New Hanover County commissioner gave him the edge.

But just as the campaign should have been picking up, powerful Hurricane Fran blew through the district on Sept. 5, devastating much of eastern North Carolina, just as the region picked up after Hurricane Bertha two months earlier.
The Seventh District -- which encompasses eight southeastern North Carolina counties -- was particularly hard hit, and the race was immediately sent to the backseat as residents struggled to rebuild.
Campaign managers have struggled to distinguish their similar candidates, and independent polls have called the race a tossup, with large numbers of undecided voters.

Caster and McIntyre have similar positions on most issues. Both oppose almost all abortions, as well as stronger gun control. Both support school prayer, oppose school vouchers, favour a bigger military budget and oppose President Clinton's plan to classify tobacco as a drug.

Given this, pundits have said the result may well hinge on one group of voters in Robeson County -- the 37,000 members of the Lumbee Indian tribe, on whom Rose fought to bestow federal recognition in each of his 12 terms.

The two candidates have even taken the same stance on Lumbee recognition. Caster has described himself as "an enthuiastic supporter." McIntyre has said the same. The Lumbees have said they will support only a candidate that commits to reintroducing the legislation when Congress reconvenes next year.
